summary.text: Lagrange's theorem says that if H is a subgroup of a finite group G, the number of elements in H divides the number of elements in G.
The quotient |G|/|H| is the index [G:H], the number of left cosets of H in G.
It helps prove Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem, and shows that any group of prime order is cyclic and simple.

facts.label: Converse fails
facts.value: The group A₄ has 12 elements but no subgroup of order 6

facts.label: Cauchy's theorem
facts.value: A subgroup exists for any prime dividing the group order

facts.label: Cosets
facts.value: Cosets of one subgroup are either identical or disjoint

facts.label: Special cases
facts.value: Fermat's and Euler's theorems were known long before

items.prompt: A finite group has 15 elements. Can it contain a subgroup with exactly 4 elements?

options.label: Yes, any size below 15 can occur
Yes, if the group is not cyclic
No, 4 does not divide 15
Only if the subgroup is normal

items.explain: The order of every subgroup divides the order of the whole group, and 4 does not divide 15.

items.prompt: A group has a prime number of elements. Why must the subgroup built from any non-identity element be the whole group?

options.label: Its size must divide the prime, so it is the whole group
Prime groups have exactly one element
Every element is its own inverse
Prime groups are always abelian by definition

items.explain: The subgroup generated by a non-identity element has more than one element and its size divides a prime, so it is the entire group, making it cyclic and simple.

items.prompt: A group has 12 elements and 6 divides 12. Must the group have a subgroup of order 6?

options.label: Yes, every divisor gives a subgroup
Yes, but only a normal one
No, but then it has two of order 3
No, the converse of the theorem can fail

items.explain: A divisor of the group order does not guarantee a subgroup of that size; the group A₄ has 12 elements and no subgroup of order 6.

items.prompt: Cosets of a subgroup split a group into pieces. If two such pieces share even one element, what must be true?

options.label: They overlap in exactly half their elements
They are the very same piece
One piece is strictly bigger than the other
They both equal the subgroup itself

items.explain: The cosets generated by a subgroup are either identical or disjoint, so any shared element means they are the same.

items.prompt: A finite group's order is divisible by the prime 5. Which partial converse of the theorem guarantees something?

options.label: Nothing can be guaranteed
A subgroup of every possible order
Only a normal subgroup of order 5
An element, and a cyclic subgroup, of order 5

items.explain: Cauchy's theorem guarantees an element, and hence a cyclic subgroup, of order any prime dividing the group order.

items.prompt: A subgroup H splits a finite group G into left cosets. How many cosets are there?

options.label: The order of G times the order of H
The order of G minus the order of H

items.explain: The quotient |G|/|H| is an integer equal to the index [G:H], the number of left cosets.

paragraphs.heading: The statement
paragraphs.text: Lagrange's theorem is about finite groups and the groups that sit inside them. If H is a subgroup of a finite group G, then the order of H divides the order of G. Here the order of a group means how many elements it has. The theorem is named after Joseph-Louis Lagrange.

paragraphs.heading: Counting cosets
paragraphs.text: A sharper version says that |G| / |H| is not just a whole number: it equals the index [G:H], which is the number of left cosets of H in G. Rearranged, this gives the equation |G| = [G : H]|H|. The cosets of one subgroup split the group into pieces, since any two of them are either identical or have no elements in common. The sharper version holds even for an infinite G, as long as the sizes are read as cardinal numbers.

paragraphs.heading: What it proves
paragraphs.text: Fermat's little theorem, and Euler's theorem that generalizes it, both follow from Lagrange's theorem. People knew those special cases long before anyone proved the general result. The theorem also shows that a group whose order is prime must be both cyclic and simple. The reason is that the subgroup generated by any element other than the identity has to be the whole group.

paragraphs.heading: Infinitely many primes
paragraphs.text: The theorem even gives a proof that the primes never run out. Suppose p were the largest prime, and take any prime q dividing the Mersenne number 2ᵖ − 1. Then 2ᵖ ≡ 1 (mod q), which means 2 has order p inside the multiplicative group (ℤ/qℤ)^(∗). By Lagrange's theorem, p must divide the order of that group, which is q − 1. That forces p < q, which contradicts p being the largest prime.

paragraphs.heading: The converse fails
paragraphs.text: A natural question is whether every divisor of a group's order is the order of some subgroup. In general the answer is no. The smallest counterexample is A₄, the alternating group of degree 4. It has 12 elements, yet none of its subgroups has 6 elements. A finite group where the answer is yes for every divisor is called a CLT group. Every CLT group must be solvable, and every supersolvable group is a CLT group.

paragraphs.heading: Partial converses
paragraphs.text: Some weaker versions of the converse do hold. For any group, Cauchy's theorem promises an element, and so a cyclic subgroup, whose order is any given prime that divides the group's order. Sylow's theorem goes further: there is a subgroup whose order is the largest power of such a prime that divides the group's order. For solvable groups, Hall's theorems give a subgroup for each unitary divisor of the group's order, meaning a divisor coprime to its cofactor.
